summary: This document specifies how to use the AES-GMAC message authentication code with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) described in RFC 5652. It defines the conventions needed so a CMS message can carry an authentication tag produced by AES-GMAC, letting a receiver check that the content was not changed.

plainLanguage.summary: A message can carry a secret stamp that proves nobody scribbled on it along the way. This document explains how to put one particular kind of stamp, called AES-GMAC, onto messages in a common secure-message format.

subtitle: The identifiers and parameters for using the AES-GMAC authentication code inside CMS messages.

tldr.problem: The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) needs agreed conventions before it can carry authentication codes produced by AES-GMAC.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9044 defines three algorithm identifiers (one per AES key size) and a GMACParameters structure with a nonce and a tag length, and explains how to compute GMAC with an AES-GCM implementation.
tldr.outcome: CMS implementations can use AES-GMAC in AuthenticatedData, as long as nonces are unique per key and the tag length stays fixed.

facts.label: Nonce size
facts.value: 8 to (2^64)-1 bits, multiple of 8; 12 octets recommended

today: RFC 9044 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2021, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the RFC Specifies
sections.content: RFC 9044 specifies the conventions for using the AES-GMAC Message Authentication Code (MAC) algorithm with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) defined in RFC 5652. A MAC lets a receiver who holds the shared key check that content was not changed. The document is short: it is mostly identifiers, a parameter structure and an ASN.1 module.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a small instruction sheet that tells everyone how to stick a particular tamper-proof seal on messages, so all programs do it the same way.

sections.title: Algorithm Identifiers and Parameters
sections.content:
In CMS, MAC algorithm identifiers go in the AuthenticatedData macAlgorithm field and MAC values go in the mac field. AES-GMAC uses one of three identifiers, chosen by the AES key size of 128, 192 or 256 bits: id-aes128-GMAC, id-aes192-GMAC or id-aes256-GMAC.

For all three, the AlgorithmIdentifier parameters field MUST be present and MUST contain GMACParameters, a SEQUENCE of a nonce and a length. The nonce is the GMAC initialization vector. It may have any number of bits between 8 and (2^64)-1 but MUST be a multiple of 8 bits, and it MUST be unique within the scope of any content-authentication key. A 12-octet nonce is RECOMMENDED because it can be processed more efficiently.

The length field is the MAC size in octets (12 to 16, default 12). It MUST match the size of the value in the mac field, and 12 octets is RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three versions of the stamp, one for each size of secret key. Each stamp comes with a never-repeated number and a note saying how long the stamp is.

sections.title: Computing GMAC from AES-GCM
sections.content:
An existing AES-GCM implementation can produce AES-GMAC. Provide the content-authentication key as the AES key, the nonce as the initialization vector, a zero-length plaintext, and the content to be authenticated as the additional authenticated data (AAD). The result, which some implementations call the authentication tag, is the AES-GMAC authentication code. Because there is no plaintext, the encryption step is skipped and no ciphertext is produced.

The DEFAULT and RECOMMENDED values in GMACParameters were chosen to align with the parameters for AES-GCM in Section 3.2 of RFC 5084.
sections.plainLanguage: If you already own a machine that scrambles and stamps, you can feed it nothing to scramble, and just keep the stamp it makes.

sections.title: The ASN.1 Module and IANA Registration
sections.content:
Section 5 gives an ASN.1 module, CryptographicMessageSyntaxGMACAlgorithms, that uses the MAC-ALGORITHM definition from RFC 5912. It defines the three object identifiers under the NIST aes arc: { aes 9 } for 128-bit keys, { aes 29 } for 192-bit keys and { aes 49 } for 256-bit keys. It also defines GMACParameters and MACLength, an INTEGER restricted to 12, 13, 14, 15 or 16, and marks each algorithm as a keyed MAC whose parameters are required.

IANA registered one object identifier for the module itself: decimal 72, id-mod-aes-gmac-alg-2020, in the "SMI Security for S/MIME Module Identifier" registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The formal rulebook writes the three stamp types and their options in a precise machine-readable language, and the official registry now lists this rulebook under number 72.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Reusing a nonce under the same key lets an attacker produce valid AES-GMAC codes for arbitrary messages, so the nonce MUST be unique per content-authentication key, and the tag length MUST be fixed within that scope. If AES-GMAC is a building block in another algorithm, it MUST be used only once by that algorithm; for example, it MUST NOT be the pseudorandom function for PBKDF2.

The key distribution method must itself provide authentication, and when more than two parties share a key, data origin authentication is not provided, since any holder can compute a valid MAC. The forgery probability is close to 2^(-t) for a tag of t bits, though GMAC strength degrades slightly with message length, so implementations SHOULD use 16-octet tags for messages over 2^64 octets. Keys must be randomly generated with a good source of randomness, and implementations should be modular to allow algorithm replacement over time.
sections.plainLanguage: Never use the same one-time number twice with the same secret, or a cheater can forge stamps. Pick secrets truly at random, and everyone who knows the secret can make stamps, so you cannot tell which of them made one.
